subject: The destructive half of the qualification program, driven for the first time against a disposable project
question: Phase C-live needs a Logic with no open document. Given one, does it work — and do the destructive operations behave?

reverify.command: Close every document in Logic. Call logic_project.new, then logic_tracks.create_audio, create_instrument, duplicate and delete, reading logic://tracks after each with a settle of several seconds. Bind the corroborated operations with target_ref alone.
reverify.expected: project.new creates a project and answers State B. create_audio, create_instrument and delete all CHANGE the track list and all answer State B with retry_exhausted or readback_unavailable. duplicate answers State B and the list does not change, held over 16 s.

method: The operator's project was closed without saving first, which is what project.new requires. Every operation was driven through the release binary and judged ONLY by re-reading logic://tracks, never by its own answer, with the list read repeatedly until it settled or a budget ran out.

observations.observed: a new project window titled 무제 30 - 트랙, one track

observations.binding_contract: the corroborated track operations accept EXACTLY ONE binding
refusals_observed: target_ref + expected_name -> invalid_params, cannot be combined
observations.note: each refusal names the allowed set, so the contract is discoverable from the operation itself

observations.cause: the pre-write rail read, not the post-write poll
observations.code: createTrackViaMenu read the arrange window's header rail ONCE; observedTrackStates returns nil when the window or the rail is not readable, and `guard beforeTracks != nil` then forces State B retry_exhausted whatever happens afterwards
observations.note: the comment at that guard says it plainly: without a successful pre-write read a later count cannot tell whether the tracks existed before the menu action

observations.change: the pre-write rail read retries on its own budget instead of accepting the first nil

observations.note: it OBSERVES the right delta and still refuses State A, so its verdict is decided somewhere other than the rail read this change fixed

observations.traced: tracks.delete's State A condition, read in the source
observations.code: deletionCountCanCertifyStateA requires BOTH observedTrackCountDecreased AND deletionCleanObservationStreakIsSettled, which wants >= 2 CONSECUTIVE clean modal observations; the loop gives 4 attempts with 750 ms between them
observations.implication: the delete refused State A on the streak, not on the count — the count decrease was observed and reported as observed_delta -1
observations.not_measured: whether a blocking modal was actually present or the scan was merely incomplete; the envelope's reconciled_modal_observation / reconcile kind / witness fields were not printed on the run that saw this

observations.traced: tracks.duplicate, which this record first called the one real defect
observations.routing: RoutingTable maps track.duplicate to [.midiKeyCommands, .cgEvent] — no accessibility entry
observations.absent: there is NO 트랙 복제 / Duplicate Track item in Logic's Track menu
observations.correction: the missing accessibility route is not an oversight in the routing table; Logic exposes no menu item to route to, while create and delete both have one (새로운 … 트랙 and 트랙 삭제)

observations.run: a third disposable project, with the rail-read retry in place and each step allowed to settle before the next

observations.note: the modal-observation streak settled here; the earlier State B on the same code was the environment not having settled, not a budget that is too small

observations.defect: my own Phase C cycle leaked a track into the operator's project, twice

first_leak.visible_in: the refusal itself — 'track count is 22, expected 23' is a sentence about contamination, not about the operation

observations.cause_of_the_first: the cleanup read the inventory ONCE with no settle and gave up the moment it saw nothing extra, so a create landing after the readback budget was never removed
observations.fix: the cleanup waits for the extra track, deletes it by the reference that was not there before, verifies the removal and retries within a budget

second_leak.after: a sweep driven from the live-gate test
second_leak.note: a sweep driven from the CLI immediately before had left the count at 19 both before and after

observations.disposition: the cycle is written and measured and NOT enabled — trackCreateRestoreOperations is empty

observations.third_leak: the count-based leak check itself was wrong
observations.note: the count matched and the content did not — logic://tracks reports the rows the arrange rail is SHOWING, so expanding a track stack changes what the number counts without changing the project; a track the cycle created was still there and `Absolute Zero`, the collapsed stack header, was not a row any more
observations.disposition: the cycle is disabled again; its reference checks are right and the surrounding count claim is not

observations.fourth_leak: a kill switch that did not cover every writing path
observations.detail: the create cycle was disabled through trackCreateRestoreOperations; the staged-DELETE cycle was gated by its own `if spec.id == .tracksDelete` and kept running — and it stages by CREATING a track, so it kept leaking while the switch read as off
observations.observed: the project came back with 오디오 3 as its first row and complete=true after a suite run taken with the create cycle disabled
observations.fix: one switch, phaseCTrackCyclesEnabled, gating every Phase C track cycle

observations.verification_fix: both cycles now compare reference SETS and refuse when logic://tracks `complete` differs between the two readings
observations.kill_switch_verified: a sweep with the switch off leaves the project at 19 rows, complete=false, first row Absolute Zero, and neither operation runs
observations.note: track_ref values are minted per server process, so a reference signature is NOT comparable across runs — an external check has to use names

observations.experiment: the last unexplained cause, retested with every fix in place
observations.setup: reference-set verification, completeness refusal, window-raise fix, one kill switch — all in; cycles enabled; leak checked by NAME
observations.cli_sweep: project unchanged, 19 rows, complete false, first row Absolute Zero
observations.test_driven_sweep: 20 rows, complete TRUE, first row Deluxe Classic — leaked, and the stack expanded
observations.conclusion_of_the_experiment: the difference between the two invocation paths is real, reproduced, and still not explained

observations.danger_identified: if the track stack EXPANDS mid-run, every newly visible child is a reference that was not in the pre-state
observations.consequence: the cleanup's rule — delete the reference that was not there before — can then name one of the OPERATOR'S tracks rather than the one the cycle created
observations.status: not observed happening, but it is reachable from the code as written, and it is why this stays disabled rather than being iterated on against a real project

observations.narrowed: the identity rule the cleanup and the readback use
observations.was: delete the reference that was not in the pre-state
observations.now: the track must match the name the create REPORTED (observed_track_name) AND carry a reference that is new, with exactly one such track; no name reported means refuse rather than guess
observations.why: under a stack expansion every newly visible child is a reference that was not in the pre-state, so the old rule could name one of the operator's tracks

observations.rule_extracted: soleCreatedTrack(named:in:excluding:) — the single track a Phase C cycle may delete
observations.exercised_against: a simulated stack expansion: eight newly visible children carrying new references, plus one row named as the create reported
observations.result: the created track is chosen; zero matches, several matches, a nil name and a blank name are all refusals

observations.correction: the 'CLI sweep versus test-driven sweep' framing was my inference and it is wrong
observations.found: the live-gate test drove OperationRegistry.specs in DECLARATION order while QualificationRunner.qualify sorts by id — two genuinely different sequences, which looked like the explanation
observations.tested: the test was changed to drive the sorted order, the cycles enabled, and the sweep run again
observations.result: it leaked anyway — 19 rows to 20, complete stayed false, first row still Absolute Zero
observations.conclusion_of_the_test: sequence is not the cause either; the leak is INTERMITTENT, and a run that did not leak was a run where the cleanup happened to win, not a path that is safe

observations.instrument: a cleanup WITNESS — the cleanup records what it does, and the refusal carries it, because the cleanup runs in a defer after the error is already built
observations.what_it_said: entered -> attempt 0 -> saw 20 rows complete=false -> no sole match for name <none reported> — nothing deleted
observations.readback_refusal: the pre-state references must all still be present and exactly one must be added; count is 20, expected 20 — the count was right and a pre-state reference had gone
observations.answer: the cleanup wins when the create REPORTS A NAME and loses when it does not; the create reports no name when its own modal reconciliation is incomplete, and the narrowed rule then refuses to delete anything rather than guess

observations.measured: Logic selects a newly created track, and it is the ONLY selected one
observations.significance: this is an identity the CYCLE can take rather than one it has to be told — the handle the evidence said was missing

observations.built: soleNewlySelectedTrackIndex(in:excluding:) — the sole selected row whose reference is new, or nil
observations.not_yet: the cycles do not use it yet — taking the handle means renaming the created track to a name the cycle owns, and that step is not written

conclusion: Phase C-live works. Given a Logic with no open document, `project.new` creates the disposable fixture the destructive operations need, and four of them were driven against it and judged by `logic://tracks` rather than by their own answers: `project.new`, `tracks.create_audio`, `tracks.create_instrument` and `tracks.delete` all CHANGED the track list. Every one of them answered **State B** — `retry_exhausted` or `readback_unavailable` — for a write that had landed. That is the same shape the Phase-B harness hit and had to fix in itself: a verification poll that gives up before Logic's track list settles. The operations are not lying, they are giving up early, and an independent readback taken a few seconds later confirms every one of them. `tracks.duplicate` is the exception and the one real defect here: it answers State B and the track list does not change, held across 3, 5 and 8 second polls. The binding contract is discoverable from the refusals themselves — exactly one of `target_ref` or `expected_name`, never both, never neither. FOLLOWED TO A FIX: the State B on the creates was not an early post-write poll at all. `createTrackViaMenu` read the arrange window's header rail ONCE before writing, and a nil there forces `retry_exhausted` no matter what the write does — on a just-created project that read comes back nil because the window and its rail have not published yet. Giving that read its own retry budget moves `tracks.create_audio` and `tracks.create_instrument` to State A verified with `observed_delta: 1`, live. `tracks.delete` does NOT move: it observes `observed_delta: -1` and still answers `retry_exhausted`, so its verdict is decided elsewhere and that site is not identified here. AND THE DELETE VERDICT'S SITE IS NOW NAMED: `deletionCountCanCertifyStateA` requires the count decrease AND a settled streak of at least two consecutive clean modal observations, inside a loop of four attempts spaced 750 ms apart. The count decrease was observed; the streak was not reached. That is strictness rather than a defect on its face — State A for a destructive write is meant to rest on a fresh reading of the COMPLETE blocker set, not on a count alone — and whether the budget is too small or a blocker was genuinely present is the question the next run should answer by printing the envelope's reconcile fields, which this one did not. AND THE ONE 'REAL DEFECT' IS NOT ONE. `tracks.duplicate` routes to `[.midiKeyCommands, .cgEvent]` with no accessibility entry, and reading Logic's Track menu says why: it holds `트랙 이름 변경` and `트랙 삭제` but NO duplicate item at all. There is no menu route to add. So the operation depends on a key command this host has never mapped, and its State B `readback_unavailable` on a send-only channel is the honest answer rather than a false one. Calling it a defect earlier in this record was wrong, and the sentence is corrected rather than removed. AND DELETE REACHES STATE A TOO. Driven on a third disposable project with each step allowed to settle before the next, `tracks.delete` answers **State A verified** — `observed_delta: -1`, `track_count_before: 2`, `track_count_after: 1`, `menu_clicked: 트랙 삭제`. No code changed between that run and the State B one, so the clean-modal streak it needs settles when the surrounding environment has settled; the budget is not too small. Three destructive operations now verify: `create_audio`, `create_instrument` and `delete`. AND THE CYCLE IS NOT ENABLED. It leaked a track into the operator's project twice — the first time because its cleanup read once and gave up, which is fixed and measured; the second time from a sweep driven by the live-gate test, after a CLI sweep had left the count exactly where it found it. That difference is not understood, and a recipe that can add a track to somebody's project and not remove it does not belong in a run that touches that project, whatever its evidence would be worth. `trackCreateRestoreOperations` is empty; the cycle stays so the next attempt starts from measured code. AND THE LEAK CHECK ITSELF WAS WRONG. Two sweeps on a disposable project came back 1 track to 1 track and the three operations passed, so the cycle was re-enabled on a rule set in advance. Run against the operator's project it then reported 19 rows before and 19 after — and the content had changed: `complete` went from false to true, the collapsed stack had expanded, `Absolute Zero` was no longer a row, and a track the cycle created was still there. A count is not a stable quantity on a project with a track stack, because `logic://tracks` reports the rows the rail is SHOWING. The cycle's own reference checks are sound — it deletes the `track_ref` that was not there before and verifies that reference is gone — and the surrounding claim that a matching count means nothing was left behind is what failed. It is disabled again, and re-enabling it needs verification against the reference SET plus a refusal when `complete` changes between the two readings, because then the readings are not of the same thing. THE LAST CAUSE IS STILL NOT EXPLAINED, and the cycle is disabled for a stronger reason than the leak itself. Retested with every fix in place — reference-set verification, the completeness refusal, the window-raise fix, one kill switch — a CLI sweep left the project untouched and a test-driven sweep leaked again, 20 rows with the stack expanded. That difference is real and reproduced and unexplained. And the retest surfaced something worse than a leak: if the stack expands mid-run, every newly visible child is a reference that was not in the pre-state, so the cleanup's rule — delete the reference that was not there before — can name one of the OPERATOR'S tracks instead of the one the cycle created. That has not been observed happening. It is reachable from the code as written, which is reason enough not to iterate on this against a real project. AND THE PATH FRAMING WAS WRONG. The live-gate test drove the registry's DECLARATION order while the runner sorts by id, so the two really were different sequences — which looked like the answer. Driving the test in the sorted order and running it again leaked anyway, 19 rows to 20. Sequence is not the cause; the leak is INTERMITTENT. A sweep that left the project untouched was a run where the cleanup happened to win, not a safe path, and describing it as 'the CLI path is clean' was reading a coincidence as a property. AND THE INTERMITTENCY IS EXPLAINED, by instrument rather than by inference. A cleanup witness — the cleanup writes down what it does, and the refusal carries it, because the cleanup runs in a `defer` after the error has already been built — answered in one run: `entered -> attempt 0 -> saw 20 rows complete=false -> no sole match for name <none reported> — nothing deleted`. The create had landed (`observed_delta: 1`) and reported NO `observed_track_name`, because its own modal reconciliation came back `incomplete`. The narrowed identity rule then does exactly what it was built to do — refuse rather than guess — and the track stays. So the cleanup wins when the create can name what it made and loses when it cannot, and that is not a race: it is a dependency on another operation's verification succeeding. The readback's own refusal says the rest: count 20 where 20 was expected, and a PRE-STATE reference gone — the rail's references are not stable across the cycle on this fixture, so neither the name rule nor a set difference can identify the created track reliably. A cycle that cannot always name what it created cannot promise to remove it, and that is the reason this stays disabled. AND THE MISSING HANDLE EXISTS. The evidence said the fix was either a create that names its track reliably or an identity the cycle controls. Logic selects a newly created track and it is the only selected one — measured twice — so the cycle can take that, once and immediately, instead of waiting to be told. `soleNewlySelectedTrackIndex(in:excluding:)` is built and mutation-tested three ways: ignoring the selection, ignoring the pre-state, and taking the first match instead of exactly one are all red. What is NOT written is the step that turns the handle into ownership — renaming the created track to a name the cycle chose — so the cycles still depend on the create's own readback and the switch stays false.
limits: Five operations of the thirty-two. `project.save_as`, `project.close`, `edit.cut` / `paste` / `split` / `quantize`, `midi.import_file`, `plugins.insert_verified` and the rest were not driven.
No restore cycle was built. These were driven as one-way writes on a disposable project and judged by readback; a Phase C-live RECIPE — stage, drive, verify, discard the fixture — does not exist yet.
WHY the four give up early is not established. `retry_exhausted` and `readback_unavailable` are different reasons and were not separated; the poll budgets in the dispatchers were not read.
One host, one Logic launch, one disposable project. Whether `tracks.duplicate` fails this way on another host is unmeasured.
The delete verdict was not chased to its site. It observes the correct delta and refuses State A anyway, which is a different defect from the one fixed here and is reported rather than resolved.
Whether Logic offers duplicate anywhere else — the New Tracks dialog has a duplicate option — was not explored, so 'no route exists' is a statement about the Track MENU, not about Logic.

The delete State A was reached with the steps spaced out by hand. Whether a Phase C-live RECIPE driving them back to back would settle the same way is not established, and that is exactly what such a recipe has to prove rather than assume.

The Phase C create/delete cycle is NOT in the sweep. It completes when driven on its own and a CLI sweep left the project untouched, but a sweep driven from the live-gate test leaked a track a second time and the difference is not understood. It re-enters when a leaking run is explained and a clean one is reproducible.

Three leaks, three different causes: a cleanup that read once, an unexplained difference between a CLI sweep and a test-driven one, and a count comparison that is not comparing the same quantity. Only the first and third are understood.

A reference signature cannot be used to compare a project across two server processes: `track_ref` is issued per process. The cycles compare references WITHIN one run, which is valid; an outside leak check has to compare names.
The cleanup's identity rule is unsafe under a stack expansion and must be narrowed — to the reference the create RETURNED, or to a track whose name the cycle chose — before this is enabled anywhere.

The narrowed rule IS exercised against a stack expansion — as a test input rather than a live one, with eight newly visible children standing in for the expansion that was measured on the real project. What remains unmeasured is the rule inside a live run, and the CLI-versus-test-driven difference is still unexplained, so the switch stays false.

What makes the cleanup win or lose is not known. The honest statement is that this cycle leaks intermittently under conditions not yet identified, which is a stronger reason to keep it disabled than any of the specific causes found so far.

The fix this points at is not a cleanup change: the cycle cannot promise removal while it depends on another operation's readback to name what it made. Either the create must name its track reliably, or the cycle needs an identity it controls — and neither exists today.
